warmup: Bluestem's bank asks for audited financial statements. Why would a bank pay attention to statements the company prepares itself?
Introduces the role of standards and independent audit in making reports credible.
acts: List three decisions that investors or creditors make using Bluestem's financial statements.
Whether to lend and at what rate; whether to buy, hold or sell shares; covenant monitoring; supplier credit terms.
Match each body to its role: SEC, FASB, PCAOB, AICPA.

SEC: legal authority over public company reporting. FASB: writes GAAP. PCAOB: audit standards and inspections for public company audits. AICPA: CPA profession, private company audit standards, CPA exam.
Use the Codification topic list to find where guidance on inventory, leases and revenue lives.
Topic 330 inventory; Topic 842 leases; Topic 606 revenue.
Bluestem reports 'adjusted EBITDA' that excludes a lawsuit settlement. What must a public company do when it presents this measure?
Reconcile it to the most comparable GAAP measure (net income) and give the GAAP measure equal or greater prominence.
Bluestem considers listing in Toronto. Name two numbers that might change if it reported under IFRS.
Inventory if it uses LIFO; property if revalued; development costs capitalized; impairment reversals.
Role-play: Sam responds to the founder's request to delay invoices. Draft his two-sentence reply.
Records the invoices in December; suggests approaching the bank for a waiver, offering to prepare a forecast.
case: The covenant squeeze

Bluestem's loan covenant requires net income of at least $500,000. Draft results show $460,000. The founder suggests three ideas: delay $40,000 of December repair invoices; record a $60,000 order shipped January 3 as December revenue; and change depreciation from 10 to 15 years for existing equipment, cutting expense by $30,000.
Which ideas violate GAAP?
Which, if any, could be acceptable, and under what conditions?
Who are the stakeholders?
What should Sam do?

Delaying invoices and recording January revenue in December violate GAAP (expenses and revenue belong to the period incurred/earned). A change in useful life is a change in estimate and acceptable only if supported by evidence about the assets, not to hit a covenant; it applies prospectively. Stakeholders: bank, owners, employees, auditor, Sam. Sam should record correctly and help the company seek a waiver.
exam: Explain the roles of the SEC, the FASB and the PCAOB in US financial reporting.

SEC: statutory authority, delegates standard setting, reviews filings, enforces. FASB: private, due process, issues ASUs into the Codification. PCAOB: created by SOX, audit standards and inspections for public company auditors.
Describe the FASB's due process and explain why it matters.
Agenda, research, discussion paper, exposure draft, comment letters and roundtables, ASU. Gives affected parties a voice, improves quality and legitimacy, despite political pressure.
outcomes: Explain the role of financial reporting in capital allocation
Identify the primary users and objective of financial reports
Describe the roles of the SEC, FASB, PCAOB and AICPA
Explain due process and use the Codification
Compare US GAAP and IFRS at a high level
Apply an ethical decision process to a reporting dilemma
take: Investors and creditors are the primary users
SEC authority, FASB standards, PCAOB audits
IFRS differs in places like LIFO
Recognize the dilemma, then weigh stakeholders

warmup: A friend says, 'Accounting is just rules.' Where would you look for an answer if no rule covers a new type of transaction?
Leads into the conceptual framework as the basis for judgment.
acts: State the objective of financial reporting in your own words and explain who it serves.
Provide information useful to investors, lenders and creditors in making capital decisions.
Classify each: (a) prior forecasts compared with actual; (b) no bias in estimates; (c) all needed information included; (d) a $3 error in $10 million of sales.
(a) Confirmatory value (relevance); (b) neutrality; (c) completeness; (d) immaterial.
Classify: kayak sales; a loss on selling an old forklift; dividends paid; the owner contributes land; wages owed at year-end.
Revenue; loss; distribution to owners; investment by owners; liability (and expense).
Name the assumption violated: (a) the founder's personal car on Bluestem's balance sheet; (b) adjusting PP&E for inflation; (c) recording wages when paid.
(a) Economic entity; (b) monetary unit; (c) accrual basis.
Assign a fair value level: (a) Apple shares; (b) corporate bonds priced from similar bonds; (c) a private startup investment valued by a model.
Level 1; Level 2; Level 3.
Bluestem's controller finds a $15,000 error. Income is $1.2 million. Is it material? What else would you consider?
1.25% of income: likely immaterial quantitatively; consider nature (fraud?), covenants, trends, segment effects.
case: The dealer incentive

Bluestem offers dealers a free kayak rack with every 10 kayaks bought in December. Sam must decide (1) whether the racks are a separate cost to record now, (2) whether to disclose a lawsuit by a customer injured in a capsized kayak (lawyers think Bluestem is unlikely to lose), and (3) whether to keep valuing a 5% stake in a local startup at cost or at a model-based fair value.
Which framework concepts apply to each issue?
How does the cost constraint affect the rack decision?
What disclosure does full disclosure require for the lawsuit?
Discuss relevance vs faithful representation for the startup stake.

Racks: expense recognition/matching (and later, revenue allocation); immaterial items may be expensed. Lawsuit: full disclosure; if loss only reasonably possible, disclose; if remote, no disclosure required (Lecture on contingencies in 312). Startup: fair value more relevant but Level 3, less verifiable; GAAP rules for equity investments decide (ACCT 312).
exam: Explain the two fundamental qualitative characteristics and their ingredients, with an example of each.
Relevance: predictive, confirmatory, materiality. Faithful representation: complete, neutral, free from error. Examples from Bluestem.
Identify and explain the five basic assumptions and give a consequence of each.
Entity (separate records), going concern (cost and depreciation), monetary unit (no inflation adjustment), periodicity (estimates and accruals), accrual basis (revenue and expense timing).
outcomes: Explain the purpose and levels of the conceptual framework
Describe the qualitative characteristics of useful information
Define the elements of financial statements
Explain the five basic assumptions
Apply the measurement, recognition and disclosure principles
Apply the cost constraint and materiality
take: Assets and liabilities define the rest
Entity, going concern, monetary unit, periods, accruals
Mixed model: cost and fair value

warmup: Bluestem paid a full year of insurance in October. If no one makes an entry at December 31, which statements are wrong, and in which direction?
Assets overstated, expenses understated, income and equity overstated: motivates adjusting entries.
acts: Record: Bluestem buys $40,000 of aluminum on account; pays $15,000 of it; sells kayaks for $90,000 cash.
Dr Inventory 40,000 / Cr AP 40,000; Dr AP 15,000 / Cr Cash 15,000; Dr Cash 90,000 / Cr Sales 90,000 (plus COGS entry under perpetual).
Bluestem pays $36,000 on August 1 for 12 months of software subscriptions. Prepare the December 31 adjustment.
5 months × 3,000 = 15,000. Dr Software expense 15,000 / Cr Prepaid 15,000.
A $80,000, 9% note payable was signed October 1. Prepare the December 31 accrual.
80,000 × 9% × 3/12 = 1,800. Dr Interest expense 1,800 / Cr Interest payable 1,800.
A truck costs $64,000, salvage $4,000, life 5 years, bought July 1. Year-1 depreciation?
Revenues $1,500,000; expenses $1,320,000; dividends $50,000. Prepare closing entries and the change in retained earnings.
Close revenue and expenses to Income Summary (180,000 net income), Income Summary to RE, dividends to RE; RE +130,000.
Cash paid for wages $410,000; wages payable rose from $6,000 to $9,000. Accrual wage expense?
case: The shoebox bookkeeping

Bluestem's new retail shop kept cash-basis records for its first year: cash sales and collections $260,000; cash paid to suppliers $140,000; cash paid for rent $30,000 (covering 15 months, starting January 1); wages paid $48,000. At year-end, customers owe $12,000, suppliers are owed $9,000, $2,000 of wages are unpaid, and inventory on hand cost $15,000.
Compute accrual-basis revenue.
Compute cost of goods sold.
Compute rent and wage expense.
Compute accrual net income and compare with cash profit.
exam: Explain why adjusting entries are needed and classify the four types, with an example of each.
Accrual basis and periodicity. Prepaid expenses, unearned revenues, accrued revenues, accrued expenses (plus estimates like depreciation).

Bluestem's unadjusted trial balance shows Prepaid insurance $24,000 (paid Oct 1, one year) and Unearned revenue $30,000 (40% earned). Wages of $12,000 are accrued. Prepare the adjusting entries and their effect on net income.
Insurance −6,000; revenue +12,000; wages −12,000; net effect −6,000.
outcomes: Describe the steps in the accounting cycle
Prepare adjusting entries for prepaid expenses and unearned revenues
Prepare adjusting entries for accrued revenues and expenses
Record depreciation and use the adjusted trial balance
Prepare closing entries
Use reversing entries and convert cash to accrual
take: Accruals record what's happened before cash

warmup: Two kayak makers each report $1 million of net income. One sold its headquarters at a $600,000 gain. Which would you rather invest in, and why?
Introduces quality of earnings and the need to separate recurring and nonrecurring items.
acts: Bluestem's profit jumped 30%, but cash from operations fell. Give two possible explanations that raise quality-of-earnings concerns.
Receivables growing faster than sales; reduced reserves or bad-debt estimates; capitalizing costs; one-time gains.
Prepare a multiple-step statement: sales $2,000,000; returns $50,000; COGS $1,170,000; selling $260,000; admin $190,000; interest expense $30,000; dividend revenue $5,000; tax 25%.
Net sales 1,950,000; GP 780,000; operating income 330,000; pretax 305,000; tax 76,250; income from continuing 228,750.
Bluestem's camping-furniture line (a strategic shift) had an operating loss of $60,000 and a $20,000 gain on sale. Tax 25%. Compute the discontinued operations amount.
Pretax loss 40,000; net loss 30,000.
Classify where each goes: storm loss; loss on discontinued segment; unrealized gain on AFS debt securities; correction of a prior-year error.
Continuing ops (pretax, separate line); discontinued ops net of tax; OCI net of tax; beginning retained earnings net of tax.
Compute EPS for Bluestem: continuing $472,500; discontinued −$90,000; 250,000 shares.
Continuing $1.89; discontinued $(0.36); net income $1.53.
Prepare a retained earnings statement: beginning $900,000; prior period adjustment (error) −$40,000 net of tax; net income $210,000; dividends $75,000.
Adjusted beginning 860,000; ending 995,000.
case: The analyst's question

An analyst reviewing Bluestem's draft 2027 statements notes: income from operations of $680,000 includes a $45,000 uninsured storm loss and $30,000 restructuring charges; net income of $382,500 includes a $90,000 loss from the fishing-boat division; and the founder wants to present 'core earnings' excluding all three items in the press release.
Recompute operating income excluding the storm and restructuring.
Is the fishing-boat division correctly reported?
Should the storm loss be reported net of tax as a separate category?
What rules govern 'core earnings' if Bluestem is public?

755,000 excluding them. Yes, as discontinued operations, net of tax, if a strategic shift. No: no extraordinary items; it stays pretax in continuing operations, separately disclosed. Non-GAAP measures must be reconciled to GAAP and not given more prominence (SEC rules).
exam: Explain the criteria and presentation of discontinued operations, and why they are reported separately.

Component disposed or held for sale; strategic shift with major effect; report operating results and gain/loss on disposal net of tax below continuing operations; EPS separately; improves predictive value.

From the following, prepare the bottom of Bluestem's income statement and EPS (300,000 shares): pretax income from continuing operations $800,000; tax 25%; discontinued operations pretax loss $100,000.
outcomes: Explain the uses and limitations of the income statement
Evaluate quality of earnings
Prepare a multiple-step income statement
Report discontinued operations and unusual items
Apply intraperiod tax allocation and compute EPS
Prepare retained earnings and comprehensive income statements
take: Income predicts cash flows, with limits
Multiple-step shows gross profit and operations
Discontinued ops: net of tax, below continuing
No extraordinary items in US GAAP
EPS on the face for public companies

warmup: Bluestem has $4 million of assets on its balance sheet. Would you pay $4 million for the company? Why or why not?
Book vs market value; omitted intangibles; historical cost.
acts: Explain liquidity, solvency and financial flexibility, and name one balance sheet item that bears on each.
Liquidity: cash, receivables. Solvency: long-term debt vs assets. Flexibility: unused credit, low leverage.
Classify: prepaid insurance (12 months); land held for speculation; patents; bond sinking fund; inventory; equipment.
Current; long-term investment; intangible; long-term investment (restricted); current; PP&E.
Classify: accounts payable; current portion of mortgage; unearned revenue; bonds due in 8 years; dividends declared; treasury stock.
Current; current; current; long-term; current; contra equity.

Compute the current, quick and debt-to-assets ratios for a company with cash $50,000, receivables $150,000, inventory $300,000, current liabilities $250,000, total liabilities $600,000, total assets $1,500,000.
Current 2.0; quick 0.8; debt to assets 40%.
Classify each cash flow: interest paid; sale of old truck; issuing common stock; purchase of equipment; collections from customers; repayment of loan principal.
Operating; investing; financing; investing; operating; financing.

Decide whether to adjust or disclose: (a) customer with a December receivable declares bankruptcy in January; (b) Bluestem issues bonds in February; (c) lawsuit from a November accident settled in January.
(a) Adjust; (b) disclose; (c) adjust (condition existed at year-end).
case: The covenant ratio

Bluestem's loan requires a current ratio of at least 2.0. On December 31, current assets are $1,400,000 and current liabilities $650,000. The founder suggests (1) using $150,000 of cash to pay down accounts payable on December 30; (2) reclassifying $200,000 of inventory as a long-term asset; (3) delaying a large aluminum purchase on account from December 29 to January 3.
Compute the current ratio after idea 1.
Is idea 2 acceptable?
Is idea 3 acceptable?
What ethical issues arise?

Idea 1: 1,250,000 ÷ 500,000 = 2.5 (legitimate; it raises the ratio when it's above 1). Idea 2: not acceptable; inventory held for sale is current. Idea 3: a genuine change in purchase timing is legal but window dressing; if goods arrived in December they must be recorded. Ethical issues: misleading the lender; disclosure of window dressing.
exam: Explain how current assets and current liabilities are defined, and give three examples of each.
One year or operating cycle, whichever longer; cash/receivables/inventory/prepaids; payables/accrued/unearned/current portion of LTD.
Using Bluestem's numbers (CFO $520,000, capex $380,000, dividends $120,000, current assets $1.4m, current liabilities $650,000), compute free cash flow and the current ratio and comment.
FCF $20,000; current ratio 2.15; adequate liquidity but limited discretionary cash; inventory-heavy.
outcomes: Explain the uses and limits of the balance sheet
Classify assets
Classify liabilities and equity
Prepare a classified balance sheet and compute liquidity and solvency ratios
Classify cash flows and compute free cash flow
Apply disclosure requirements, including subsequent events
take: Current = one year or operating cycle
Current portion of debt is current
Notes are part of the statements

warmup: Would you rather receive $100,000 today or $130,000 in five years? What does your answer depend on?
The interest rate (opportunity cost) and risk; sets up present value.
acts: Identify the rate per period and number of periods: (a) 10% compounded semiannually for 4 years; (b) 9% compounded quarterly for 3 years.
(a) 5%, 8 periods; (b) 2.25%, 12 periods.
Bluestem deposits $75,000 today at 8% compounded annually. How much in 6 years? (factor 1.58687)
A dealer gives Bluestem a $90,000 non-interest-bearing note due in 3 years. Market rate 6% (factor 0.83962). How much revenue does Bluestem record now?
$75,566 revenue; $14,434 interest over 3 years.
What rate makes $40,000 grow to $59,200 in 5 years? (FV factors, 5 periods: 7% 1.40255; 8% 1.46933)
Required factor 1.48: about 8.2%, just above 8%.
Bluestem will deposit $20,000 at the end of each year for 10 years at 7% (FVA factor 13.81645). Fund balance? If deposits are at the start of each year?
A lease requires $25,000 at the start of each year for 4 years at 6% (PVA ordinary factor 3.46511). Present value?
case: Buy or lease the paint line

Bluestem can (A) pay $165,000 cash for the paint line today; (B) pay $40,000 at the end of each year for 5 years; or (C) pay $38,000 at the start of each year for 5 years. Bluestem can borrow at 8%. (PVA ordinary, 5 periods, 8% = 3.99271.)
Compute the present value of B.
Compute the present value of C.
Which option is cheapest?
How would Bluestem record option B on the balance sheet?
B: $159,708. C: 38,000 × 4.31213 = $163,861. A: $165,000. B is cheapest. Record equipment and a note payable at $159,708; interest expense recognized over 5 years.
exam: Explain the difference between an ordinary annuity and an annuity due, and show how to convert an ordinary annuity factor into an annuity due factor.
Payment timing at end vs beginning; multiply ordinary factor by (1 + i) for both FV and PV.
Bluestem must accumulate $600,000 in 8 years. It can earn 5% (FV of 1 factor 1.47746; FVA ordinary factor 9.54911). (a) Single deposit today? (b) Equal end-of-year deposits?

Distinguish simple and compound interest
Compute future and present values of single sums
Solve for unknown rates and periods
Compute future values of ordinary annuities and annuities due
Compute present values of annuities

Match the rate to the period
Factor = FV ÷ PV to find rate or time
Record assets at PV; the rest is interest

warmup: A lottery winner can take $1 million today or $80,000 a year for 20 years. Which would you choose, and what would you need to know?
Discount rate, timing, taxes, risk; previews annuities and comparing streams.
acts: A note pays $20,000 a year for 5 years, first payment at the end of year 4. Value at 6% (PVA 5 = 4.21236; PV of 1, 3 periods = 0.83962).
Price a 4-year, $200,000 bond with a 5% stated rate paid semiannually when the market rate is 6% (8 periods at 3%: PV of 1 = 0.78941; PVA = 7.01969).
Prepare the first two interest entries for the bond in activity 2 (investor).
Period 1: interest 5,789 (192,980 × 3%); cash 5,000; amortization 789; carrying 193,769. Period 2: interest 5,813; amortization 813; carrying 194,582.
Bluestem borrows $150,000 for 4 years at 6% with equal annual payments (PVA factor 3.46511). Compute the payment and the year-1 interest and principal.
Payment $43,288; interest $9,000; principal $34,288; balance $115,712.
Expected cash flow: a warranty obligation payable in 2 years: 40% $50,000, 40% $70,000, 20% $100,000. PV at 4% risk-free (factor 0.92456).
Expected 68,000; PV $62,870.
Midterm warm-up: name the timing error in each: (a) annuity due treated as ordinary; (b) semiannual bond discounted annually.
(a) Understates PV/FV by one period of interest; (b) wrong rate and periods (use half rate, double periods).
case: The design license

Bluestem is offered two deals for its kayak design license. Deal 1: $85,000 cash today. Deal 2: $30,000 a year for 4 years, starting at the end of year 3, plus a $20,000 signing payment at the end of year 1. Bluestem's discount rate is 8%. (PV of 1 at 8%, 1 period: 0.92593.)
Value deal 2.
Which deal is better?
What non-financial factors matter?
How would Bluestem record deal 2 at signing?

Deal 2: 85,189 + 18,519 = $103,708 > $85,000. Deal 2 is better financially, but carries credit risk of the licensee over 6 years; consider currency and enforcement. Record a receivable at present value $103,708 (if revenue recognized at signing) and accrue interest over time.
exam: A $500,000, 10-year bond pays 8% interest semiannually. The market rate is 10%. Compute the price (20 periods at 5%: PV of 1 = 0.37689; PVA = 12.46221) and the first period's interest using the effective-interest method.
Principal 188,445 + interest 20,000 × 12.46221 = 249,244; price $437,689. Interest 21,884; amortization 1,884.
Explain the expected cash flow approach and when it is preferable to the traditional approach.
Probability-weighted cash flows discounted at risk-free rate; preferable when cash flows are uncertain in amount or timing (AROs, contingencies, impairment).
outcomes: Value deferred annuities
Price bonds from their cash flows
Apply the effective-interest method
Compute loan payments and amortization
Apply the expected cash flow approach
Integrate the first half of the course
take: Expected flows use a risk-free rate

warmup: Bluestem's sales rose 20% but cash collections rose only 5%. What might be happening with receivables?
Slower collections, looser credit, possible aggressive revenue; sets up valuation and turnover.
acts: Which are cash or cash equivalents: currency; 2-month Treasury bill; 6-month CD; postdated check; money market fund; travel advance to an employee?
Cash/equivalents: currency, T-bill, money market fund. Not: CD (ST investment), postdated check (receivable), travel advance (receivable).
Record a $40,000 sale on 2/10, n/30 expected to be paid early, then collection after 20 days.
Dr AR 39,200 / Cr Sales 39,200; Dr Cash 40,000 / Cr AR 39,200, Cr Sales discounts forfeited 800.
Aging: current $200,000 (1%), 1–60 days $50,000 (10%), over 60 days $20,000 (40%). Allowance has a $4,000 debit balance. Required allowance and expense?
Required 15,000; expense 19,000.
Record a $6,000 write-off, and its later recovery. What happens to net receivables at each step?
Dr Allowance / Cr AR (no change); reinstate then collect (no change to net AR, cash up and AR down).
Bluestem accepts a $240,000 zero-interest note due in 3 years; market rate 6% (factor 0.83962). Record the sale and year-1 interest.
Revenue 201,509; interest 12,091.
Factor $150,000 without recourse: 2% fee, 4% holdback. Compute cash, the loss and the entry.
Cash 141,000; due from factor 6,000; loss 3,000.
case: The spring cash crunch

Bluestem has $450,000 of receivables and needs $300,000 by March. Option A: a bank loan secured by receivables at 9%. Option B: factor $320,000 of receivables without recourse (4% fee, 5% holdback). The founder prefers B because 'it keeps debt off the balance sheet and improves our current ratio.' Bluestem's current ratio is 2.15 (current assets $1.4m, current liabilities $650,000).
Compute cash, loss and holdback under B.
Compute the current ratio under A (borrow $300,000 short-term) and under B (receivables removed; cash and the holdback receivable added).
Is the founder's reasoning sound?
What must be true for B to be a sale?

B: fee 12,800, holdback 16,000, cash 291,200. A: CA 1,700,000 / CL 950,000 = 1.79. B: CA 1,400,000 − 320,000 + 291,200 + 16,000 = 1,387,200 / 650,000 = 2.13. B does avoid the liability, but costs a 4% fee on short-term money; sale treatment requires surrendering control (isolation, transferee can pledge/sell, no effective control).
exam: Explain the CECL model and prepare the adjusting entry from an aging schedule requiring $30,000 when the allowance has an $8,000 credit balance.
Lifetime expected credit losses using history, current conditions, forecasts; expense 22,000; net receivables at amount expected to be collected.
Bluestem sells equipment for a $300,000 zero-interest note due in 3 years when the market rate is 8% (factor 0.79383). Record the sale and interest for years 1 and 2.
Revenue 238,149; year-1 interest 19,052; carrying 257,201; year-2 interest 20,576.
outcomes: Identify what is reported as cash and cash equivalents
Record receivables with cash discounts
Estimate credit losses with an aging schedule under CECL
Record write-offs and recoveries
Record notes receivable at present value
Account for transfers of receivables and compute turnover
take: Sale only if control is surrendered

warmup: A kayak is sitting at a dealer's showroom in Duluth. Whose inventory is it? What would you need to know?
Consignment vs sale; control; sets up which goods to include.
acts: Classify: aluminum sheets; fully assembled kayaks; kayaks awaiting painting; cleaning supplies for the factory; kayaks held by a dealer on consignment.
Raw materials; finished goods; WIP; supplies (or overhead); finished goods (Bluestem's).
Periodic: beginning inventory $90,000; purchases $410,000; freight-in $6,000; purchase returns $8,000; ending inventory $110,000. COGS?
Net purchases 408,000; available 498,000; COGS 388,000.

Adjust a count of $300,000: goods sold FOB destination still in transit to a customer $12,000 (not counted); goods bought FOB destination in transit $8,000 (not counted); Bluestem goods at a consignee $5,000.
Record a $20,000 purchase on 2/10, n/30 under the net method, then payment after 15 days.
Dr Inventory 19,600 / Cr AP 19,600; Dr AP 19,600, Dr Purchase discounts lost 400 / Cr Cash 20,000.
Ending inventory 2027 was overstated $15,000. Show the effects on 2027 and 2028 COGS, income and retained earnings (ignore tax).
Inventory grew 35% while sales grew 8%. List three questions you'd ask management.
Obsolete stock? Count/cutoff problems? Production for an expected order? Changes in costing method? Channel stuffing reversals?
case: The year-end count

Bluestem's count team reports $732,000. Sam's cutoff review finds: aluminum costing $15,000 shipped by a supplier FOB shipping point on December 29, arriving January 3; kayaks costing $22,000 at three dealers on consignment; paddles costing $9,000 held for a supplier on consignment; and kayaks costing $18,000 sold FOB shipping point on December 31, shipped that day, that were (correctly) not counted, but the sale was recorded on January 2.
Compute correct inventory.
What's wrong with the December 31 shipment, and its effect on income?
Record the correction (sales price $28,800).
Recommend a control.

Inventory 760,000. The sale should be recorded in December: revenue and receivable understated by 28,800; COGS understated by 18,000 if perpetual not updated; income understated by 10,800. Dr AR 28,800 / Cr Sales 28,800; Dr COGS 18,000 / Cr Inventory 18,000 (if perpetual still shows it). Control: match shipping documents to invoices around year-end.
exam: Explain how goods in transit and consigned goods are treated, with examples.
FOB shipping point: buyer's when shipped; FOB destination: seller's until delivered; consigned goods stay with consignor until sold.
Explain the effect of an understated 2027 ending inventory of $22,000 on 2027 and 2028 financial statements.
2027: COGS over, NI under, RE under, current assets under. 2028: COGS under, NI over; RE correct by end of 2028.
outcomes: Classify inventories for manufacturers and merchandisers
Compare perpetual and periodic systems
Determine which goods belong in inventory
Determine which costs are inventoried
Analyze the effects of inventory errors
Recognize inventory fraud risks and controls

warmup: A gas station's tanks mix every delivery together. Which cost flow assumption best describes what physically happens?
Average cost; physical flow needn't match the assumption.
acts: Using Bluestem's touring kayak data, compute COGS and ending inventory under weighted average.
Average $428; ending 128,400; COGS 299,600.
Compute FIFO ending inventory and COGS for: beginning 50 at $20; purchases 100 at $22, 150 at $25; 180 units sold.
Ending 120 at $25 = 3,000; available 6,950; COGS 3,950.
Compute periodic LIFO ending inventory and COGS for the same data.
Moving average (perpetual): beginning 100 at $10; sell 60; buy 100 at $13; sell 80. Ending inventory?
After first sale 40 at $10 = 400; purchase → 140 units, 1,700, avg 12.143; sell 80 → 60 units ≈ $729.
FIFO inventory $900,000; LIFO $760,000 at year-end; reserve was $110,000 last year. Compute the reserve and the year's LIFO effect.
Reserve 140,000; LIFO effect +30,000 to COGS.
A LIFO competitor reports COGS of $3,000,000; its LIFO reserve rose from $300,000 to $500,000 during the year. Restate its COGS to FIFO for comparison.
case: The method decision

Bluestem's paddle division has steadily rising costs (about 6% a year) and no plans to list outside the US. FIFO COGS this year would be $1,100,000; LIFO COGS $1,160,000. The tax rate is 25%. The bank's covenant requires net income of at least $500,000; projected income before the method choice is $540,000 under FIFO.
Compute income under each method.
Compute the cash tax saving from LIFO.
Does LIFO breach the covenant?
Recommend a method.

Pretax difference 60,000; after-tax 45,000. LIFO income 495,000 (if 540,000 is after-tax FIFO income): below covenant. Tax saving 15,000 a year. Options: negotiate covenant on a FIFO basis (many lenders allow LIFO reserve add-back) and use LIFO for the tax saving; or stay FIFO. Conformity rule requires LIFO in books if used for tax.

case: Choosing a method for the new line

Bluestem's new kayak-thermoforming line costs $600,000, salvage $60,000, life 6 years or 54,000 hours. Expected use: heavy in years 1–3 (12,000 hours each), then 6,000 hours a year. The founder wants straight-line because 'it gives the best income in year 1'. The bank covenant uses EBITDA.
Compute year-1 depreciation under SL, SYD, DDB and activity.
Which method best reflects the pattern of use?
Does the method matter for the covenant?

SL 90,000; SYD 6/21 × 540,000 = 154,286; DDB 1/3 × 600,000 = 200,000; activity $10/hour × 12,000 = 120,000. Activity best reflects use (heavy early). EBITDA excludes depreciation, so the covenant is unaffected. Recommend activity (or accelerated) for matching; SL acceptable but less representative.

case: The fishing-boat molds

At December 31, 2027, Bluestem's fishing-boat molds (cost $500,000, accumulated depreciation $200,000) are used for one dealer whose orders fell 70%. Projected undiscounted cash flows are $240,000; fair value is $180,000. In 2028, Bluestem decides to sell them; carrying amount is then $150,000, fair value $140,000, costs to sell $8,000. The founder argues that the 2027 loss should be avoided 'because the dealer may recover'.
Test for impairment at December 31, 2027 and record any loss.
What is depreciation in 2028 if the remaining life is 6 years and salvage is zero?

Evaluate the founder's argument.

Loss 120,000; new basis 180,000; 2028 depreciation 30,000 (carrying 150,000). Held for sale: 132,000; loss 18,000; stop depreciating. The founder's hope isn't evidence; GAAP requires the test using best estimates; no reversal later.
exam: Explain the US GAAP impairment model for assets held for use and compare it with assets held for sale and with IFRS.

Two-step: recoverability (undiscounted) then FV; no reversal. Held for sale: lower of CA or FV − costs to sell, no depreciation, recoveries allowed. IFRS: one-step recoverable amount, reversals allowed.
